question.text: The point $(-1, 1)$ lies on the curve $y = f(x) + 1.$ Which of the following points must lie on $y = -f(x) - 1?$
question.explanation:
Method 1

To plot $y = -f(x) -1,$ we apply the following steps:

  • First, take the graph $y = f(x) + 1.$

  • Then, we shift the graph vertically by $1$ unit down and get the graph of $y=f(x).$ After this transformation, the point $(-1,1)$ will be mapped to the point \[ (-1,1-1)=(-1,0). \]

  • Next, we reflect the result across the $x$-axis and get the graph of $y=-f(x).$ After this transformation, the point $(-1,0)$ will be mapped to the point \[ (-1,-(0)) = (-1,0). \]

  • Finally, shift the result vertically by $1$ unit down and obtain the graph of $y = -f(x) - 1.$ After this transformation, the point $(-1,0)$ will be mapped to the point \[ (-1,0-1)=(-1,-1). \]

Method 2

Since the point $(-1, 1)$ lies on the graph of $y = f(x)+1$, we have that

\[ f(-1)+1 = 1 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad f(-1)=0. \]

Now consider the graph of $y = -f(x) -1.$ Substituting $x = -1$, we get

\begin{align*} y &= -f(-1) -1 \\[3pt] &= -0-1 \\[3pt] &= -1. \end{align*}

Therefore, the point $(-1, -1)$ must lie on $y = -f(x) - 1.$

question.text: The point $(0, 1)$ lies on the curve $y = f(x+2).$ Which of the following points must lie on $y = -f(x) + 2?$
question.explanation:
Method 1

We first find a point corresponding to $(0,1)$ on $y=f(x).$ Then, we find a corresponding point on $y=-f(x)+2\mathbin{:}$

  • To plot the graph of $y=f(x),$ we apply the following steps:

    • First, take the graph $y = f(x+2).$

    • Then, we shift the graph horizontally $2$ unit to the right and get the graph of $y = f(x).$ After this transformation, the point $(0,1)$ will be mapped to the point \[ (0+2,1)=(2,1). \]

  • Next, to plot the graph of $y = -f(x) + 2,$ we apply the following steps:

    • First, take the graph $y = f(x).$

    • Then, we reflect the result across the $x$-axis and get the graph of $y=-f(x).$ After this transformation, the point $(2,1)$ will be mapped to the point \[ (2,-(1)) = (2,-1). \]

    • Next, we shift the result vertically by $2$ units up and obtain the graph of $y = -f(x) + 2.$ After this transformation, the point $(2,-1)$ will be mapped to the point \[ (2,-1+2)=(2,1). \]

Method 2

Since the point $(0, 1)$ lies on the graph of $y = f(x+2)$, we have that

\[ f(0+2) = 1 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad f(2)=1. \]

Now consider the graph of $y = -f(x) + 2.$ Substituting $x = 2$, we get

\begin{align*} y &= -f(2) + 2 \\[3pt] &= -(1) + 2 \\[3pt] &= 1. \end{align*}

Therefore, the point $(2,1)$ must lie on $y = -f(x) + 2.$

question.text: The diagram above shows the global minimum and maximum of the function $y=f(x).$ What is the global minimum of $y=-2f(x+1)?$
question.explanation:
Notice that the graph of $y=-2f(x+1)$ can be obtained from the graph of $y=f(x)$ by

  • translating it by $1$ unit to the left, then

  • stretching it by a scale factor of $2$ parallel to the $y$-axis, and finally

  • flipping it across the $x$-axis.

Since one of these transformations flips the graph across the $x$-axis, the combined transformation maps the global maximum of $y=f(x)$ to the global minimum of $y=-2f(x+1).$ So, we need to find the image of $(-1,4),$ the global maximum of $y=f(x),$ under the transformation.

To plot $y=-2f(x+1),$ we apply the following steps:

  • First, we take the graph $y=f(x)$ that passes through $(-1,4).$

  • Then, we shift the graph horizontally by $1$ unit to the left and get the graph of $y=f(x+1).$ After this transformation, the point $(-1,4)$ will be mapped to the point
    \[ (-1-1,4) = (-2,4). \]

  • Next, we stretch the result by a scale factor of $2$ along the $y$-axis and get the graph of $y=2f(x+1).$ After this transformation, the point $(-2,4)$ will be mapped to the point
    \[ (-2,2 \cdot 4) = (-2,8). \]

  • Finally, we flip the result vertically across the $x$-axis and get the graph of $y = -2f(x+1).$ After this transformation, the point $(-2,8)$ will be mapped to the point \[ (-2,-1 \cdot 8) = (-2,-8). \]

Therefore, the global minimum of $y=-2f(x+1)$ is $(-2,-8).$
